messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh’s trauma began thirty years ago when his five-year-old daughter Linh was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. He spent every evening at the children’s hospital after work, sitting by her bedside as the antiseptic smell of the ward—bleach, iodine, hand sanitizer—clung to his clothes. What he could never shake was the sound of the IV pump and the sight of doctors performing lumbar punctures and bone marrow aspirations. Those months became a blur of fear and helplessness, but the memory itself never blurred: it stayed razor-sharp and immediate, as if he were still there, a film that played over and over no matter how many years passed.

Decades later, at seventy-five, Minh works part-time as a cybersecurity analyst. The job demands periodic health screenings, and just a routine blood draw now sends his heart racing and his palms sweating—a strong physical reaction he cannot control. The moment the nurse swabs his arm with an alcohol pad, the hospital smell hits him, and suddenly he is back in that sterile room, watching Linh’s small body stiffen in pain. These triggers do not just provoke anxiety; they pull the entire memory into the present, making it feel as if it is happening right now rather than something long over. The smell, the sight of the needle—they are the direct doorway to the film that plays over and over.

After a particularly vivid flashback at work—Minh had briefly lost track of where he was, believing for a moment that he was again at Linh’s bedside—he found himself hyperaware of every antiseptic smell in the building. The memory had primed him to detect triggers that he might otherwise have ignored. That evening, a whiff of hand sanitizer from a colleague sent him reeling again. The memories themselves were creating a world full of triggers, so that even a faint hospital odor on a passing stranger’s clothes could start the cycle anew.

What frightened Minh most was the way his own fear amplified the memory. The moment his chest tightened with dread, the memory would snap into sharper focus—the exact shade of the hospital curtain, the sound of the monitor alarms—as if his body’s alarm system was rewinding the film. He had come to believe that if he could just stop the physical reaction, he could keep the memory at bay, but the opposite seemed true: the stronger his fear, the more the memory consumed him, pulling him deeper into the past.

He avoided any mention of hospitals, changed the channel when medical dramas appeared, and could not bear to visit his daughter when she was pregnant, because seeing her belly triggered images of the neonatal intensive care unit where other babies had fought for life. This avoidance had cost him precious time with his family; his daughter had felt hurt by his distance during her pregnancy. But Minh was certain that his presence would only lead to a full-blown flashback, and he had learned that when the memory flooded back, it was impossible to explain to anyone what had happened. When he tried to describe it, he lost the thread and could not finish a sentence.

Finally, after his annual physical—a required procedure for his job—left him trembling and disoriented for two days, his daughter insisted he see a therapist. Minh comes now because he is tired of being a prisoner to a past that feels more real than the present. He is afraid that the memory will never fade, but he is also hoping that someone can help him find a way to live without feeling like he is still in that hospital room.
